dimension_justifications.soundness: Arithmetic that can be checked from the paper checks out, and the paper is disciplined about labelling what is measured versus re-expressed: Appendix C (pp. 19-21) rebuilds every Store row from the format identity bytes(n,b)=ceil(n/64)(8b+4), reproduces the printed 56.438 MiB full-prefix-Q8 to 0.002 MiB, and factors the headline 5.84x exactly into 3.9174x (split) x 1.4912x (bit width), conceding that only the first is a split-replay effect. But the claim the paper now leads with is the total-memory claim, and that one is extrapolated rather than measured. Table 1 (p. 8) and the Conclusion (p. 9, 'the claim is capacity-first: smaller total memory for a large warm set') rest on three assumptions the authors themselves mark unverified - S linear in D with 'no run held more than one document resident', T independent of D 'unverified', and fits licensed only for N in [1,8] from four points - and the table's own footnote states 'No workload of the many-warm-document shape these rows describe was executed.' Every directly measured system comparison runs against the method: transient allocation is higher at all four fanouts (Table 5, p. 21), TTFT and throughput are worse than exact reuse, dense recomputation, SGLang Radix and HYPIC (Sec. 5.3, p. 6; Tables 22-24, pp. 35-37), and the ownership component 'saves nothing' against the paper's own paged-prefix baseline (Sec. 5.5, p. 8). Further substantive gaps, all disclosed but none repaired: the throughput column reconciles with no generated-token count (Table 22 note, p. 35); the eight-item dense TPOT of 648.75 ms equals its own TTFT while the operating-point dense arm reads 53.46 ms, 'a discrepancy we flag and do not reconcile' (Sec. 5.7, p. 9); the headline policy was selected on the panel that evaluates it with no multiplicity adjustment across ten pairwise intervals (Appendix B, p. 16); F1 is a reimplementation of qa_f1_score with two stated behavioural deviations (Sec. 5.1, p. 5); and the primary ForkAudit factorial never ran on the packed Read path behind Tables 4 and 22 (Sec. 5.7, p. 9). The core is plausible and honestly bounded, but the gap between what was measured and what is concluded is decision-changing, which is a 2 under this rubric rather than a 3.
dimension_justifications.presentation: Structure is logical and every caveat is findable, but density materially obstructs evaluation. The abstract (p. 1) is one unbroken ~65-line paragraph carrying roughly thirty numeric quantities, five nested concessions, two confidence intervals, a crossover point and a regime statement; a reader cannot extract the contribution boundary from it without reading Sections 5.2-5.6 first. The three contribution bullets (pp. 2-3) repeat the same construction. Four separate executions with four different memory denominators (Sec. 5.1, p. 5) force constant cross-referencing, and the reader must hold 'Store, BF16 ref.' versus 'Store, native' versus the Sec. 5.5 allocator denominator versus the Sec. 5.6 CUDA-allocator transient peak simultaneously to read Table 4 (p. 20) and Table 1 (p. 8) together. Appendix tables are out of order - Table 22 is typeset on p. 35 before Table 21 on the same page, and the body's Table 1 depends on appendix Tables 4 and 5. Figures 1-3 are clear and Figure 1's caption honestly annotates that the drawn Read path is not the one behind the deployment tables. Thirty-plus tables across 34 appendix pages is a lot of surface for a nine-page contribution, and it dilutes rather than supports the argument.
dimension_justifications.contribution: The paper disclaims, correctly and explicitly, nearly every mechanism it uses: the split-replay primitive (CoMem, Liu et al. 2026a;b), group-wise asymmetric quantization (Jacob et al. 2018; Sheng et al. 2023), layer-wise mixed-precision bit assignment (KVTuner, AsymKV), quantize-an-intermediate-and-recompute (XQuant), block sharing and copy-on-write (PagedAttention), prefix reuse (SGLang, Prompt Cache), hybrid prefix caching (Marconi, HYPIC), recurrent-state quantization (Quamba, Quamba2, MambaQuant), and each individual audit mechanism (Table 16, p. 32). What remains is a conjunction of specifics - a depth-j boundary residual packed together with lower-layer attention KV and GDN convolution/recurrent state, reported under a whole-entry denominator - plus an ownership regression harness. Novelty asserted at that level of specificity is real but narrow, and it is weakened in three ways. First, two closer prior works are absent from the bibliography (HCache, EuroSys 2025; Shirokikh and Nikolenko, Sparse Prefix Caching for Hybrid and Recurrent LLM Serving, arXiv Apr 2026), one of which directly contradicts the paper's 'XQuant is the closest prior work' claim. Second, the paper never places its numbers beside those of the method it extends: no CoMem arm is run and no CoMem-denominator ratio is printed, even though Table 3 (p. 19) makes it computable. Third, the two contributions beyond the accounting are, by the paper's own measurements, near-null: the composition run shares 2 of 16 tensors and 0.500 of 12.938 MiB (~4%) and 'demonstrates the ownership discipline ... not a memory saving' on a code path that is not the deployed one (Sec. 5.6, p. 8; Sec. 5.7, p. 9), and ForkAudit's detection increment is 'transition-time localization, not exclusive detection' because a conventional persistent-base content invariant also catches the historical alias (Table 18, p. 32). There is genuine new knowledge here - the measured refutation of the authors' own transient-memory prediction, and the clean split-versus-width decomposition of a compression ratio - but it is narrow, negative-leaning, and bounded to one model, one hardware and one operating point. That is 'narrow, incremental, weakly positioned' = 2.

paper_summary: Q-CoMem extends CoMem-style depth-split replay to a hybrid (full-attention plus Gated-DeltaNet) backbone. Offline, a Write step runs a document through layers [0,j) and group-quantizes the depth-j boundary residual together with the lower-layer attention KV and GDN convolution/recurrent state under per-layer, per-state-type bit widths (frozen policy: Q4 residual, Q4 layer-3 attention KV, Q8 GDN, at j=7). Online, a Read step dequantizes the entry, exposes immutable document tensors, creates request-local mutable state, replays the query through the lower layers, and reconstructs the suffix [j,L). The ownership boundary is validated by ForkAudit, a phase-indexed storage/call trace with seven contract targets (plus three packed-entry obligations), evaluated on a 96-configuration full-prefix BF16 vLLM factorial and separately on an eight-item composition run that shares one packed entry across N<=8. Evaluation is on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B / H20-3e over 60 Qasper and 2WikiMQA items. Reported: retained state falls from 106.235 to 9.661 MiB/document (10.9965x; 14.10x against the stack's native FP32-GDN entry) at -0.45 [-2.06, 0.99] mean F1; peak transient allocation is higher than the exact cache at every measured fanout (930.91 vs 286.44 MiB at N=1), with fitted lines crossing only at N=12.5; the sum M_total(D,N)=S*D+T(N) favours Q-CoMem only above roughly five warm documents at low concurrency and two at N=8. Latency is worse than exact reuse, dense recomputation, SGLang Radix and HYPIC throughout, and the paper makes no latency claim.
strongest_verified_contribution: The decomposition of a compression ratio into the part attributable to the method and the part attributable to confounds, executed against the authors' own interest. Section 5.2 and Appendix C (pp. 6, 21) take the headline 5.84x advantage over a quantized exact cache and factor it exactly into 3.9174x from split depth and 1.4912x from bit width, state that 'only the former is a split-replay advantage', note that the width-matched 37.846 MiB/document arm 'was never executed' and 'carries no F1, no interval, and no claim', and separately separate the 14.10x physical reduction into a packing component and a dtype-narrowing component (30.000 of 136.235 MiB is FP32 GDN excess over BF16). The same discipline appears in Section 5.6, where a measured transient-allocation result refutes the authors' own published arithmetic prediction and is printed as such. Whether or not one accepts the method, this ratio-hygiene is a transferable methodological contribution for the KV-cache-compression literature, where product ratios against unmatched references are routine.
strengths: Attribution is explicit and, for the works it does cite, accurate. Section 2 (p. 3) names XQuant as prior art on quantize-and-recompute and states 'we claim the hybrid entry and its accounting, not quantize-and-recompute'; I verified XQuant (arXiv 2508.10395) does cache quantized layer-input activations X and rematerialize K/V during decode, so the characterisation is correct rather than a strawman. Appendix G Table 15 (p. 31) and Table 16 (p. 32) attribute each mechanism work-by-work and state that no individual audit mechanism is claimed as new.

The contribution boundary is stated in the negative as well as the positive. The abstract explicitly claims 'no lower total process memory, measured recall, edge-device performance or broad quality preservation'; Section 5.3 states 'We make no latency claim'; Section 5.5 states the ownership component 'saves nothing' against the appropriate baseline. Papers in this area rarely name their own null results this plainly.

Negative and self-refuting results are printed rather than averaged away. Table 5 (p. 21) shows Q-CoMem's transient allocation above the exact cache at every measured fanout, contradicting the component-inventory prediction the authors had previously published, and Appendix C (p. 20) retains the refuted prediction 'only because we published it'. Table 22b (p. 35) prints per-repeat min/median/max, exposing a 404.01 ms TPOT maximum against a 53.45 ms median and a four-to-five-token generation length against a 32-token cap, and then concludes the timing evidence is 'weaker, not stronger'.

Denominators are separated and never silently merged. Section 5.1 (p. 5) distinguishes four memory denominators, states that Store excludes allocator pools, process/NVML memory and workspace, and Section 5.7 states that reducing Store 'does not by itself prove lower peak VRAM or serving capacity'. Table 23's footnote (p. 36) even discloses that the SGLang-side and in-process Store estimands differ and bounds the discrepancy at 0.58% on the one object both stacks hold.

Comparison against published systems is against their real behaviour, not a strawman: SGLang 0.5.17 Radix (0.146 s TTFT) and the official HYPIC codebase's prefix cache (0.072 s) are run on the identical eight items and hardware and both beat Q-CoMem's 0.673-0.674 s, and this is reported in the body rather than an appendix.

Appendix B (p. 16) publishes all 52 paired-bootstrap intervals including the nine that cross zero, names the RNG generator and index-drawing order needed to reproduce percentile endpoints, and states that the one interval excluding zero does so by 0.0390 points and is 'evidence neither that the effect is large nor that it is robust'.
questions: HCache (Gao, Chen and Shu, 'Fast State Restoration in LLM Serving with HCache', EuroSys 2025) stores intermediate hidden states for cached contexts and recomputes the KV cache from them, in the same persisted-document/reused-across-requests serving setting as yours. On what basis is XQuant, rather than HCache, 'the closest prior work to our core mechanism' (Sec. 2, p. 3)?

Shirokikh and Nikolenko, 'Sparse Prefix Caching for Hybrid and Recurrent LLM Serving' (arXiv, Apr 2026) stores exact recurrent state at sparse checkpoint positions and recomputes the suffix - a store-versus-recompute trade-off for exactly the hybrid state families you address, along the position axis instead of the depth axis. How does depth-axis splitting compare, and does the ownership problem of Sec. 4.3 arise there too?

Table 3 (p. 19) gives the residual alone as 14.8721 MiB/document, so a CoMem-style residual-only entry would be 14.87 MiB unquantized and 4.18 MiB at Q4 - the latter well below your frozen policy's 9.661 MiB. Since your first contribution is precisely that CoMem's denominator understates the deployed hybrid entry, why is that comparison never printed, and what does the whole-entry requirement cost relative to CoMem's own reported numbers?

Is any part of the depth-split-plus-suffix-replay mechanism new relative to Liu et al. 2026a;b, or is the entire mechanical delta the quantizer applied to a larger set of tensors? A one-paragraph statement of exactly which components are inherited and which are added would let a reader size the contribution without access to a workshop paper and a preprint.

Section 5.6 concedes the composition run's Read path is 'token-identical but not identical in implementation' to the one behind Tables 4 and 22, so ownership on the deployed path 'transfers by design argument'. What specifically prevents running ForkAudit on the deployed private-materialization path itself, and would doing so cover the three packed-entry obligations on the code that produced the headline numbers?

Table 1's crossover analysis assumes S is linear in D although 'no run held more than one document resident'. What blocks a run holding, say, D in {1,2,4,8} documents resident to test that assumption and the T-independent-of-D assumption directly? Absent that, is the total-memory framing defensible as the paper's headline?

ForkAudit is positioned only against metamorphic testing, CRADLE, MT-DLComp and DNNMem. Why is it not placed against the ownership/aliasing literature whose vocabulary it borrows - ownership type systems, and dynamic alias/race detection via shadow memory - which would sharpen what the phase-indexed storage witness adds?

issues.location: Section 2, p. 3 ('XQuant is the closest prior work to our core mechanism'); Appendix G 'The two differences from XQuant', p. 30; Table 15 row 'XQuant', p. 31; bibliography pp. 11-14
issues.observed_evidence: Section 2 states 'XQuant is the closest prior work to our core mechanism: it caches quantized layer-input activations and rematerializes keys and values during decode ... so persisting a quantized intermediate and paying recomputation to avoid retaining downstream state is already its thesis.' Table 15 repeats this: XQuant is 'Closest prior art on the quantize-an-intermediate-and-recompute idea'. Appendix G's 'The two differences from XQuant' argues the delta is (a) a depth-j boundary rather than a layer input and (b) a heterogeneous hybrid entry. HCache (Gao, Chen and Shu, 'Fast State Restoration in LLM Serving with HCache', EuroSys 2025, arXiv 2410.05004) is absent from the bibliography entirely. HCache persists intermediate hidden states for cached contexts - roughly half the size of the KV cache - and recomputes the KV cache from them on a cache hit, in precisely the persisted-document, reused-across-requests serving setting this paper targets, not inside a single decode step. It is therefore closer to Q-CoMem on the dimension Appendix G uses to distance XQuant (difference (a)), leaving only difference (b), the hybrid state families, standing.
issues.why_it_matters: The paper's positioning rests on an explicitly asserted superlative - 'the closest prior work' - that a reviewer can falsify with one uncited reference. Since the paper's stated novelty is the conjunction 'depth-boundary cut PLUS heterogeneous hybrid entry', removing the first conjunct from the novelty budget halves the claimed delta and makes the contribution 'apply established quantization to the hybrid state families a known store-an-intermediate-and-recompute design would need'. This is exactly the pattern my lens is asked to police: novelty asserted because prior work used different wording (layer input, hidden state, boundary residual) for the same design move. It also matters practically: HCache reports a store/recompute trade-off with published ratios that would let the reader calibrate whether Q-CoMem's 3.9174x split factor is competitive.
issues.required_fix: Cite HCache in Section 2 and add a row to Table 15. Either withdraw the 'closest prior work' superlative in favour of 'among the closest', or defend it explicitly against HCache on a stated dimension (e.g. one boundary versus per-layer hidden states; heterogeneous hybrid entry versus dense KV restoration; quantized versus unquantized storage). Restate the two-difference argument in Appendix G so that difference (a) is scoped against a serving-time hidden-state cache, not only against a within-decode activation cache. Run a related-work sweep for the store-an-intermediate-and-recompute family and report what it returned, since a search that missed HCache is likely to have missed neighbours.
issues.verification_test: Grep the revised bibliography for HCache and read the revised Section 2 paragraph and Table 15 row; confirm that the superlative is either removed or accompanied by a named dimension on which Q-CoMem is closer to HCache than HCache is, and that Appendix G's difference (a) is restated in terms that survive a serving-time hidden-state cache.
issues.evidence_needed: A revised Section 2 and Appendix G with HCache cited and distinguished, plus a stated related-work search protocol (queries, databases, date) for the intermediate-state-plus-recomputation family.

issues.location: Abstract p. 1; Table 1 and its footnote, p. 8; Section 5.6 'Total memory, and the regime it names', p. 8; Conclusion, p. 9
issues.observed_evidence: The paper's own framing is that total memory, not the retained term, is the decision quantity ('the retained term alone is half the budget', Conclusion p. 9), and the final claim is 'capacity-first: smaller total memory for a large warm set'. That claim is supported entirely by Table 1, whose footnote states three unmeasured assumptions - 'S linear in D (no run held more than one document resident); T independent of D (unverified); fits valid only for N in [1,8]' - and closes with 'No workload of the many-warm-document shape these rows describe was executed.' Section 5.6 adds 'The setting it suits is the opposite, many documents warm and each queried intermittently, which we describe qualitatively only, having run no benchmark, task or trace of that shape.' Every directly measured comparison in the paper runs the other way: transient allocation is worse at N=1,2,4,8 (Table 5, p. 21), TTFT and throughput are worse than five separate baselines (Sec. 5.3, p. 6), and the ownership component ties or loses against the paper's own paged-prefix baseline (Sec. 5.5, p. 8).
issues.why_it_matters: This is the load-bearing significance claim, and it sits entirely on extrapolation from a single-document-resident, N<=8, one-model measurement. The novelty that survives the paper's own disclaimers - the composed hybrid split-replay entry - is only decision-relevant in the regime the extrapolation names, and that regime was never executed. As it stands the paper's new knowledge for an ICLR audience reduces to 'in every regime we measured, this composition loses; in one we did not measure, arithmetic says it wins'. Honest labelling makes this reportable, but it does not make it a demonstrated capability, and the ICLR question 'does the work contribute new, relevant, impactful knowledge or practical value' is answered mostly by the negative results rather than by the claimed contribution.
issues.required_fix: Execute a multi-document-resident workload - D in {1,2,4,8,16} warm documents at N in {1,4,8} on the same stack - and report measured S(D) and T(N,D) rather than a fitted sum of two separately measured terms. If that is out of reach, demote the total-memory regime claim from abstract and conclusion to a clearly labelled projection and make the paper's headline the measured results: the retained-term reduction with its width/dtype decomposition, and the measured adverse transient and latency terms.
issues.verification_test: Check that Table 1's cells are recomputed from directly measured M_total at each (D,N) point rather than from S*D + T(N), and that the crossover D values fall inside the measured D range; or, if demoted, check that the abstract and conclusion no longer assert a smaller total memory as a result.
issues.evidence_needed: A residency sweep over D with per-configuration measured total allocator peak and retained payload, at a minimum spanning the reported crossovers (D around 2 to 6) and one point well above them.

issues.location: Section 2, p. 3 ('Gated Delta Networks, Jamba, Marconi and HYPIC supply the hybrid architectures and reusable hybrid prefixes, stored unquantized'); Appendix G 'The established quantization surfaces', p. 30; Table 15, p. 31
issues.observed_evidence: The paper characterises the hybrid-caching prior art as systems that store reusable hybrid prefixes 'unquantized' (GDN, Jamba, Marconi, HYPIC), and Appendix G says established quantization surfaces 'pack one state family ... produced on a single execution path, whereas a hybrid split-replay entry mixes a boundary residual, lower-layer attention KV, and mutable convolution and recurrent state'. Shirokikh and Nikolenko, 'Sparse Prefix Caching for Hybrid and Recurrent LLM Serving' (arXiv 2605.05219, Apr 2026) - uncited - stores exact recurrent states at a sparse set of checkpoint positions and, on a cache hit, resumes from the deepest stored checkpoint and recomputes the remaining suffix exactly. That is the same retain-less-and-recompute-more trade-off for the same mutable recurrent state families, along the position axis rather than the depth axis, and it predates this submission by roughly five months. Separately, decay-aware and mixed-precision recurrent-state quantization for Gated-DeltaNet-class models is an active line (e.g. arXiv 2608.27513, arXiv 2608.30386) which, being roughly concurrent with this submission, I do not require be cited but which bears on how unoccupied the claimed design space is.
issues.why_it_matters: Section 2's framing gives the impression of an unoccupied quadrant - hybrid state is stored, and stored unquantized, so quantizing a partial hybrid entry is new. A prior work that already trades hybrid recurrent-state retention against suffix recomputation occupies the neighbouring cell of that quadrant and raises the obvious comparison the paper never makes: for a fixed retained-byte budget, is a depth-axis split better or worse than a position-axis checkpoint? Without it the reader cannot tell whether the depth axis is the right axis, which is the paper's central design choice and the one thing it inherits rather than justifies.
issues.required_fix: Cite Shirokikh and Nikolenko, add it to Table 15, and state in Section 2 how depth-axis splitting relates to position-axis recurrent checkpointing - in particular whether the ownership problem of Sec. 4.3 arises there, and whether the two are complementary or competing at a fixed byte budget. Soften 'stored unquantized' to describe only the four systems it actually describes, rather than the hybrid-reuse literature as a whole.
issues.verification_test: Read the revised Section 2 paragraph and Table 15 row; confirm the design space is described in terms of two axes (depth and position) with the prior work on each, and that no sentence implies the store-less-recompute-more trade-off for hybrid recurrent state is first done here.
issues.evidence_needed: Revised related work; ideally a qualitative or measured comparison of retained bytes versus recomputation cost for a depth split at j=7 against a position checkpoint at comparable retained bytes on the same stack.

issues.location: Contributions bullet 1, p. 2; Section 4.1, p. 4 ('Counting only h_j^D would understate the deployed state'); Table 3, p. 19; Table 4, p. 20
issues.observed_evidence: The first contribution is stated as whole-entry accounting against a prior method that used a narrower denominator: 'CoMem retains only the residual, unquantized in BF16, so every number here uses the whole-entry denominator.' Every ratio in the paper is then taken against full-prefix (1.00x reference in both blocks of Table 4), and no CoMem arm is executed or priced. Table 3 makes the missing comparison computable: the boundary residual alone is 14.8721 MiB/document at the cohort mean length, so a residual-only CoMem entry is 14.87 MiB unquantized and 4.18 MiB at Q4, against Q-CoMem's frozen 9.661 MiB whole entry and 28.683 MiB unquantized split entry. In other words, against the method it directly extends, Q-CoMem's unquantized split entry is roughly 1.9x LARGER and its quantized entry is roughly 2.3x larger than a same-width residual-only entry - because it must also retain the lower attention KV and GDN state. That number appears nowhere in the paper.
issues.why_it_matters: The paper's central rhetorical move is that an honest denominator is larger than the prior work's. That move is only complete if the resulting number is placed beside the prior work's number, which is what tells the reader what the hybrid requirement actually costs and what CoMem's published ratios would have to be discounted by. Printing only ratios against full-prefix means the paper's honest-denominator argument is used to justify a bigger denominator without ever being applied to the comparison it was introduced for. For a novelty-and-positioning assessment this is the difference between 'we correct a prior work's accounting' (a real, checkable contribution) and 'we assert a prior work's accounting was wrong' (an unpriced claim). It also leaves open whether the deployed contribution over CoMem is positive at all on the retained term.
issues.required_fix: Add a CoMem-denominator row to Table 4 - residual-only retained payload at native dtype and at the frozen policy's residual width - clearly labelled as a re-expression, not a run, in exactly the way the all-BF16 column and the 37.846 MiB point are labelled. State the resulting ratio explicitly in Section 4.1 or 5.2, including that it runs against the method. If CoMem's own published reduction ratio is available, state what it becomes under the whole-entry denominator.
issues.verification_test: Confirm Table 4 contains a residual-only row consistent with Table 3's 14.8721 (native) and 4.1828 (Q4) MiB/document entries, and that Section 4.1 or 5.2 states the whole-entry-versus-residual-only ratio in the text with its direction named.
issues.evidence_needed: No new run required - the components are already in Table 3; a re-expressed row plus one sentence of interpretation suffices. A measured CoMem arm on the same cohort would be stronger.

issues.location: Contributions bullet 3, p. 2-3; Section 5.5 'Allocator endpoints under a controlled ownership factor', p. 8; Section 5.6, p. 8; Section 5.7, p. 9; Table 18, p. 32; Table 19, p. 33
issues.observed_evidence: The third claimed contribution is 'Ownership-safe reuse, now audited on the packed path too.' By the paper's own measurements this contribution has no demonstrated benefit on any axis. (i) Memory: at N=32 'the audited fork ties this paper's own paged-prefix baseline exactly (2.229 GiB final, 2.843 GiB peak) and is 1.950 against 0.019 GiB worse on generation increment' (Sec. 5.5, p. 8; Table 19), and the advertised 54.5%/42.2% reduction is against a full-copy control that 'no serving engine' would use (Appendix H, p. 33). (ii) Detection: Table 18 shows a conventional persistent-base content invariant fails on all eight pre-fix cells, i.e. it catches the historical alias too, so 'the increment is transition-time localization, not exclusive detection'. (iii) Coverage: the primary 96-configuration factorial is full-prefix BF16 with no split and no quantization and 'no verdict of that factorial covers those packed entries' (Sec. 5.1, p. 5); the composition run that does cover them shares 2 of 16 tensors and 0.500 of 12.938 MiB per request (~4%), 'demonstrates the ownership discipline ... not that sharing materially reduces per-request memory', and runs a borrowing Read path that is 'token-identical but not identical in implementation' to the deployed one, so ownership on the deployed path 'transfers by design argument' (Sec. 5.7, p. 9).
issues.why_it_matters: A contribution with no memory benefit, no exclusive detection capability, and no coverage of the code path behind the paper's own headline tables is close to vacuous as a stated contribution, however honestly it is bounded. Listing it as one of three contributions inflates the apparent scope of the paper without adding decision-relevant knowledge, which is the mirror image of the overclaiming the rest of the paper carefully avoids. There is a defensible narrower contribution here - a phase-indexed storage witness schema (Appendix E) that localizes an aliasing defect to owner/layer/family at transition time, which a content invariant does not do - but that is a debugging-tooling contribution, and the paper does not position it against the ownership-typing or dynamic alias/race-detection literature that would tell a reader whether the schema itself is new.
issues.required_fix: Restate contribution 3 as what the evidence supports: a phase-indexed ownership witness schema that localizes aliasing faults at transition time, validated on a full-prefix BF16 factorial and demonstrated once on a packed borrowing path, with no measured memory or detection advantage over conventional invariants plus block sharing. Move the composition run from a headline contribution to a scope-closing validation. Add positioning against ownership type systems and dynamic alias/shadow-memory detectors so the reader can judge whether the schema, rather than its application, is novel.
issues.verification_test: Read the revised contribution bullet and confirm it names the null results (ties the paged-prefix baseline; content invariant also catches the alias; 4% shared) inline rather than deferring them to Sections 5.5-5.6, and that Appendix G Table 16 gains a row for the alias/ownership-checking literature.
issues.evidence_needed: No new experiment required; a rewritten contribution statement and one added related-work paragraph. A measurement showing ForkAudit catches a defect class that content invariants plus output equality both miss would upgrade the contribution instead of narrowing it.

issues.location: Section 2, p. 3; contributions p. 2; bibliography entries Liu et al. 2026a (COLM 2026 Workshop on Efficient Reasoning) and 2026b (arXiv 2607.28263), p. 12
issues.observed_evidence: The split-replay primitive the paper explicitly does not claim is credited to a COLM 2026 workshop paper and an arXiv preprint. Neither is a peer-reviewed archival venue. The paper states its delta over CoMem in two sentences ('we build on that interface rather than claiming a new split-replay primitive, and add quantizing the residual and the lower KV/recurrent state a hybrid model needs under an explicit storage denominator') and never enumerates which components are inherited. I was able to confirm from the arXiv abstract that CoMem does write context through an intermediate layer and recompute the query-conditioned upper layers, so the disclaimer is honest; but I could not verify from this PDF what CoMem does or does not do about hybrid backbones, mutable state, or storage accounting.
issues.why_it_matters: The entire contribution is defined as a delta over a work the reviewer cannot vet at ICLR's evidentiary standard. If CoMem already addressed any part of the hybrid entry or the whole-entry denominator, the residual novelty shrinks further; if it did not, the paper deserves the credit it claims - and a reviewer cannot tell which. This is a positioning transparency gap rather than misconduct.
issues.required_fix: Add a short paragraph or table row enumerating exactly which components of Write, Read, the storage accounting and the evaluation protocol are inherited from Liu et al. 2026a;b and which are introduced here, at the granularity of Sections 4.1-4.3.
issues.verification_test: Check that the revision contains an inherited-versus-added enumeration and that each 'added' item is traceable to a section of this paper.
issues.evidence_needed: An inherited/added component table; ideally a CoMem baseline arm on the same cohort (see I4).

issues.location: Abstract, p. 1; contributions, pp. 2-3; appendix table ordering, pp. 34-35
issues.observed_evidence: The abstract is a single unbroken paragraph of roughly 65 lines carrying about thirty numeric quantities, two confidence intervals, a fitted crossover, four worked deployment points and at least eight explicit disclaimers, with sentences such as 'but that ratio is width-confounded, factoring into 3.918x split and 1.491x bit width, and no width-matched exact cache was executed; this is a selected trade-off point, not selection-corrected, and not a statistical-equivalence claim.' The contribution bullets repeat the construction. In the appendix, Table 22 is typeset on p. 35 above Table 21 on the same page, and the body's Table 1 depends on appendix Tables 4 and 5.
issues.why_it_matters: The paper's honesty is its main asset, and the density hides it: a reader who stops at the abstract cannot identify the contribution boundary, and a reader who does not reach Section 5.6 will not learn that the total-memory claim is a projection. Density is also the mechanism by which a genuinely narrow contribution can read as a broad one, which is a positioning risk even where no individual sentence overclaims.
issues.required_fix: Rewrite the abstract to at most twelve sentences: the problem, the mechanism, the one retained-term result with its two confounds named, the one adverse transient result, the regime statement flagged as a projection, and the disclaimed set. Move the numeric inventory to Section 5. Reduce the three contribution bullets to one claim each. Fix the appendix float ordering.
issues.verification_test: Count sentences and distinct numerals in the revised abstract; confirm a reader can state the contribution boundary and the projection status of the total-memory claim from the abstract alone. Confirm appendix tables appear in numeric order.

ethics_concerns: No ethics concerns. The work uses public PG-19 and LongBench-v1 (Qasper, 2WikiMQA) data, involves no human subjects, and includes an ethics statement (p. 10) that correctly notes it assesses no safety, bias or privacy property and that efficiency gains can increase deployment scale. The Use of Large Language Models statement (p. 10) is present and unusually specific about the scope of LLM assistance and author responsibility. Third-person citation of the authors' likely own prior work (CoMem) is standard practice under double-blind review and does not by itself deanonymize; I found no anonymity violation in the PDF.
llm_usage_disclosure: This review was produced by an automated LLM-based reviewer (Claude Opus 5) operating under the R51-REV-1 novelty_positioning role in pdf_only access mode. The manuscript PDF was read in full (all 43 pages) via text extraction plus visual inspection of figure and table pages; no LaTeX source, repository, evidence file, sibling directory, prior review or author note was accessed. External web search and page fetches were used to verify five positioning claims against primary sources: XQuant (arXiv 2508.10395), CoMem (arXiv 2607.28263), HCache (EuroSys 2025 / arXiv 2410.05004), Sparse Prefix Caching for Hybrid and Recurrent LLM Serving (arXiv 2605.05219), and DAMP (arXiv 2608.27513). All scores, issue severities and recommendations were assigned by the model under the supplied ICLR 2026 rubric; no human reviewer independently verified them.
evidence_that_would_raise_score: A multi-document-resident execution (D in {1,2,4,8,16} warm documents at N in {1,4,8}) that measures M_total directly and confirms the crossovers of Table 1 inside the measured range, converting the paper's headline from a projection into a result (addresses I2).

Section 2 and Table 15 revised to cite and distinguish HCache and Sparse Prefix Caching for Hybrid and Recurrent LLM Serving, with the 'closest prior work' superlative either withdrawn or defended on a named dimension, plus a stated related-work search protocol (addresses I1, I3).

A CoMem-denominator row in Table 4 (residual-only, native and Q4) with the resulting ratio stated in the text including its direction, so that the whole-entry accounting contribution is priced against the method it corrects (addresses I4).

A width-matched exact-cache arm actually executed (the 37.846 MiB/document point at the frozen policy's own widths) with F1 and a paired interval, showing whether the F1 ordering over the quantized exact cache survives at matched precision.

Any evidence that ForkAudit catches a defect class that a persistent-base content invariant plus output equality both miss - which would convert contribution 3 from a localization tool into a detection capability (addresses I5).
A second backbone or a second hardware platform for the retained-state and transient measurements, converting a single-stack point estimate into a claim with some generality.
A timing panel with enough repeats and a generation protocol that does not stop at four to five tokens, so that the online cost of split replay is characterized rather than merely bounded as adverse.
evidence_that_would_lower_score: Discovery that CoMem (Liu et al. 2026a;b) already reports a whole-entry or hybrid-state denominator, or already applies quantization to the retained residual, which would eliminate contribution 1's remaining delta.

A further uncited prior work that already packs a partial hybrid entry (boundary state plus lower attention KV plus recurrent state) at mixed low-bit widths, which would leave the paper with the accounting and the audit alone.
Any sign that the three Table 1 assumptions fail - for example, measured T growing with D, or S not additive across resident documents - since the paper's only favourable regime is derived from them.

Evidence that the composition run's borrowing Read path differs from the deployed private-materialization path in a way that affects ownership, which would remove the 'transfers by design argument' bridge and leave the deployed path unaudited.

Unresolvable inconsistency in the timing panels beyond what is already flagged - for instance if the unreconciled throughput column or the 648.75 ms versus 53.46 ms dense TPOT discrepancy indicates a harness fault that also affects the Store or F1 columns.
Confirmation that the F1 reimplementation's two stated deviations materially change the reported deltas relative to the upstream LongBench-v1 module.
review_limitations: PDF-only access: I could not inspect the LaTeX source, the anonymous supplement, the claim/evidence map, or any archived artifact, so every provenance and replay statement in Appendices A and J is taken on the paper's word and is outside what I verified.

CoMem (Liu et al. 2026a;b) and HYPIC (Liu et al. 2026c) are a workshop paper and preprints; I confirmed CoMem's split-and-recompute mechanism from its public abstract but could not verify its denominators, its hybrid coverage, or the exact boundary between it and this submission.

My external checks establish that HCache and Sparse Prefix Caching exist and are relevant; I read their abstracts and summaries, not their full texts, so the precise degree of overlap with Q-CoMem's mechanism should be settled by the authors in rebuttal rather than assumed from my characterisation.

As the novelty and positioning reviewer I did not attempt independent verification of the statistical procedures, the allocator instrumentation, or the ForkAudit trace semantics beyond reading them for consistency with the positioning claims; the soundness and rigor roles should be weighted more heavily on those.

Concurrent work (DAMP, arXiv Aug 2026; dasc, arXiv Aug 2026) appeared within days of this manuscript's timestamp and is noted as context only; I do not require its citation and did not weight it in scoring.
